name: Introduction
text: **Welcome to DAGGERHEART,** _a collaborative fantasy tabletop roleplaying game of incredible_ _magic and heroic, heartfelt adventure._

name: What Is This?
text:
This is the Daggerheart SRD (System Reference Document). It is a repository of the mechanical elements of the Daggerheart system, edited and organized for clarity, conciseness, and quick reference.

You can use this SRD in several ways:

- To quickly look up Daggerheart’s rules-as-written during gameplay sessions.
- To ensure any homebrew content you create or publish conforms with Daggerheart’s core ruleset.
- To provide copy text made available by Darrington Press for your own publications under their Community Gaming License (www.darringtonpress.com/license).
- To better understand the mechanics of Daggerheart, absent the flavor and setting information, so you can bend or break them in the process of making your own content.

The Daggerheart SRD is not a replacement for the core rulebook, which contains setting information, additional examples of various gameplay elements, and tons of great advice for playing Daggerheart—not to mention gorgeous artwork and layout.

In short, it is Daggerheart, the system, boiled down to the bones—a lean and clean offering without all the flavor, style, and supporting material that makes the core rulebook such an evocative and enjoyable read. We hope this document proves useful to your table. Happy adventuring!

name: What Is Daggerheart?
text:
Daggerheart is a tabletop roleplaying game for one Game Master (“GM”) and 2–5 players. Each game session lasts about 2–4 hours, and Daggerheart can be played as a one-shot or a multi-session campaign of any length.

During a session of Daggerheart the GM describes situations, narrates events, and controls any adversaries or obstacles that the Player Characters (“PCs”) encounter. The players, in turn, roleplay their PCs’ reactions to the scenario presented by the GM. If the outcome of a player’s action depends on fate or fortune, the GM calls for an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}.

When a player makes an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, they utilize {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}}—two differently colored 12-sided dice (“d12s”) representing {{term:hope|Hope}} and {{term:fear|Fear}}. The {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}} are rolled, relevant modifiers are added to the results, and the total is compared to a {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} set by the GM. If the total meets or beats the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}}, the player succeeds. If it’s lower, they fail. In addition, the situation changes based on which Duality Die rolls higher, either giving the player helpful {{term:hope|Hope}} tokens or generating terrifying {{term:fear|Fear}} tokens for the GM.

name: The Golden Rule
text: The most important rule of Daggerheart is to make the game your own. The rules included in this SRD are designed to help you enjoy the experience at the table, but everyone has a different approach to interpreting rules and telling stories. The rules should never get in the way of the story you want to tell, the characters you want to play, or the adventures you want to have. As long as your group agrees, everything can be adjusted to fit your play style. If there’s a rule you’d rather ignore or modify, feel free to implement any change with your table’s consent.

name: Rulings Over Rules
text:
While playing Daggerheart, the GM and players should always prioritize rulings over rules. This SRD offers answers for many questions your table may have about the game, but it won’t answer all of them. When you’re in doubt about how a rule applies, the GM should make a ruling that aligns with the narrative.

For example, Daggerheart has a weapon called a grappler that lets you pull a target close to you. If you try to use it to pull an entire castle, the weapon text doesn’t forbid you from doing that—but it doesn’t make sense within the narrative. Instead, the GM might rule that you pull a few bricks out, or pull yourself toward the wall instead.

Similarly, if your character does something that would logically result in immediate death—such as diving into an active volcano without protection—you might not get to make one of Daggerheart’s {{term:death-move|death moves}}, which normally give you control of your character’s fate in their final moments. This kind of consequence should be made clear before the action is completed, and it should always follow the logic of the world.

As a narrative-focused game, Daggerheart is not a place where technical, out-of-context interpretations of the rules are encouraged. Everything should flow back to the fiction, and the GM has the authority and responsibility to make rulings about how rules are applied to underscore that fiction.

name: Character Creation
text:
Unless their table chooses to use pre-generated characters, each player creates their own PC by making a series of guided choices. Some of these decisions are purely narrative, meaning they only appear in or affect the game through roleplaying, but others are mechanical choices that affect the things their PC is able to do and which actions they’re more (or less) likely to succeed at when making moves and taking action.

**_Note:_** _You can fill in your character’s name, pronouns, and_ _Character Description details at any point of the character_ _creation process._

name: Step 1
text:
**Choose a Class and Subclass.** **Classes** are role-based archetypes that determine which class features and **{{term:domain-card|domain cards}}** a PC gains access to throughout the campaign. There are 13 classes in this SRD: Assassin, Bard, Brawler, Druid, Guardian, Ranger, Rogue, Seraph, Sorcerer, Warlock, Warrior, Witch, and Wizard.

- Select a class and take its corresponding **character sheet** and **character guide** printouts. These sheets are for recording your PC’s details; you’ll update and reference them throughout the campaign.
- Every class begins with one or more unique **class** **feature(s),** described at the bottom left of each class’s character sheet. If your class feature prompts you to make a selection, do so now.
- **Choose a Subclass** **Subclasses** further refine a class archetype and reinforce its expression by granting access to unique **subclass** **features.** Each class comprises two subclasses. Select one of your class’s subclasses and take its **Foundation** card.

name: Step 2
text:
**Choose Your Heritage.** Your character’s **heritage** combines two elements: **ancestry** and **community.**

- A character’s **ancestry** reflects their lineage, impacting their physicality and granting them two unique **ancestry** **features.** Take the card for one of the following ancestries, then write its name in the Heritage field of your character sheet: Aetheris, Clank, Drakona, Dwarf, Earthkin, Elf, Emberkin, Faerie, Faun, Firbolg, Fungril, Galapa, Giant, Gnome, Goblin, Halfling, Human, Infernis, Katari, Orc, Ribbet, Simiah, Skykin, Tidekin. To create a Mixed Ancestry, take the top (first-listed) ancestry feature from one ancestry and the bottom (second-listed) ancestry feature from another.
- Your character’s **community** represents their culture or environment of origin and grants them a **community** **feature.** Take the card for one of the following communities, then write its name in the Heritage field of your character sheet: Duneborne, Freeborne, Frostborne, Hearthborne, Highborne, Loreborne, Orderborne, Reborne, Ridgeborne, Seaborne, Slyborne, Underborne, Warborne, Wanderborne, Wildborne.

name: Step 3
text:
**Assign Character Traits.** Your character has six traits that represent their physical, mental, and social aptitude:

- **{{term:agility|Agility}}** (Use it to Sprint, Leap, Maneuver,etc.) A high {{term:agility|Agility}} means you’re fast on your feet, nimble on difficult terrain, and quick to react to danger. You’ll make an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll to scurry up a rope, sprint to cover, or bound from rooftop to rooftop.
- **{{term:strength|Strength}}** (Use it to Lift, Smash, Grapple, etc.) A high {{term:strength|Strength}} means you’re better at feats that test your physical prowess and stamina. You’ll make a {{term:strength|Strength}} Roll to break through a door, lift heavy objects, or hold your ground against a charging foe.
- **{{term:finesse|Finesse}}** (Use it to Control, Hide, Tinker, etc.) A high {{term:finesse|Finesse}} means you’re skilled at tasks that require accuracy, stealth, or the utmost control. You’ll make a {{term:finesse|Finesse}} Roll to use fine tools, escape notice, or strike with precision.
- **{{term:instinct|Instinct}}** (Use it to Perceive, Sense, Navigate, etc.) A high {{term:instinct|Instinct}} means you have a keen sense of your surroundings and a natural intuition. You’ll make an {{term:instinct|Instinct}} Roll to sense danger, notice details in the world around you, or track an elusive foe.
- **{{term:presence|Presence}}** (Use it to Charm, Perform, Deceive, etc.) A high {{term:presence|Presence}} means you have a strong force of personality and a facility for social situations. You’ll make a {{term:presence|Presence}} Roll to plead your case, intimidate a foe, or capture the attention of a crowd.
- **{{term:knowledge|Knowledge}}** (Use it to Recall, Analyze, Comprehend, etc.) A high {{term:knowledge|Knowledge}} means you know information others don’t and understand how to apply your mind through deduction and inference. You’ll make a {{term:knowledge|Knowledge}} Roll to interpret facts, see the patterns clearly, or remember important information.

When you “roll with a trait,” that trait’s modifier is added to the roll’s total. Assign the modifiers +2, +1, +1, +0, +0, −1 to your character’s traits in any order you wish.

name: Step 4
text:
**Record Additional Character Information.**

- Characters start a new campaign at **level 1.** Record your level in the designated space at the top of your character sheet.
- **{{term:evasion|Evasion}}** represents your character’s ability to avoid damage. Your character’s starting {{term:evasion|Evasion}} is determined by their class and appears directly beneath the {{term:evasion|Evasion}} field on your character sheet; copy this number into the {{term:evasion|Evasion}} field.
- **{{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} ({{term:hit-points|HP}})** are an abstract measure of your physical health. Your starting {{term:hit-points|HP}} is determined by your class and is recorded on your character sheet.
- **{{term:stress|Stress}}** reflects your ability to withstand the mental and emotional strain of dangerous situations and physical exertion. Every PC starts with 6 {{term:stress|Stress}} slots.
- **{{term:hope|Hope}}** is a metacurrency that fuels special moves and certain abilities or features. Each PC starts with 2 {{term:hope|Hope}}; mark these in the {{term:hope|Hope}} field of your character sheet.

name: Step 5
text:
**Choose Your Starting Equipment.**

Choose your **weapon(s):**

- Select from the Tier 1 Weapon Tables either a **two-handed** **primary weapon** or a **one-handed primary weapon and a** **one-handed secondary weapon.**Then equip your selection by recording it in the Active Weapon field of your character sheet.
- At level 1, your **{{term:proficiency|Proficiency}}** is 1; write this number in the {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} field on your character sheet, then calculate and record your **damage roll** by combining your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} value with your equipped weapon(s) **damage dice.** _Example: If your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} is 1 and your weapon’s damage_ _dice is d6+1, your damage roll is 1d6+1. {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} only_ _determines how many damage dice you roll, and does not_ _affect any flat damage modifiers._

Choose and equip one set of **armor** from the Tier 1 Armor Table, then record its details in the **Active Armor** field of your character sheet.

- Add your character’s level to your equipped armor’s **Base** **Thresholds** and record the total for both numbers in the corresponding fields. At character creation, your level is 1.
- Record your **{{term:armor-score|Armor Score}}** in the field at the top left of your character sheet. Your {{term:armor-score|Armor Score}} is equal to your equipped armor’s **Base Score** plus any permanent bonuses your character has to their {{term:armor-score|Armor Score}} from other abilities, features, or effects.

Add the following items to the **Inventory** fields on your character sheet:

- A torch, 50 feet of rope, basic supplies, and a handful of gold (mark one box in the left-hand column of your character sheet titled “Gold > Handfuls”)
- EITHER a Minor Health Potion (clear 1d4 {{term:hit-points|Hit Points}}) OR a Minor Stamina Potion (clear 1d4 {{term:stress|Stress}})
- One of the class-specific items listed on your character guide
- If applicable, whichever class-specific item you selected to carry your spells
- Any other GM-approved items you’d like to have at the start of the game

name: Step 6
text:
**Create Your Background.** Develop your character’s **background** by answering the **background questions** in your character guide, modifying or replacing them if they don’t fit the character you want to play.

_Note: Your background has no explicit mechanical effect,_ _but it greatly affects the character you’ll play and the prep_ _the GM will do. Throughout character creation, you can_ _adjust choices you made in earlier steps to better reflect this_ _background as your character takes shape. If you wish, you_ _can leave your character’s past more ambiguous for the time_ _being and discover their backstory through play._

name: Step 7
text:
**Create Your {{term:experience|Experiences}}.** An {{term:experience|Experience}} is a word or phrase used to encapsulate a specific set of skills, personality traits, or aptitudes your character has acquired over the course of their life. When your PC makes a move, they can spend a {{term:hope|Hope}} to add a relevant {{term:experience|Experience}}’s modifier to an action or {{term:reaction-roll|reaction roll}}.

- Your PC gets two {{term:experience|Experiences}} at character creation, each with a +2 modifier.
- There’s no set list of {{term:experience|Experiences}} to choose from, but an {{term:experience|Experience}} can’t be too broadly applicable and it can’t grant your character specific mechanical benefits, such as magic spells or special abilities. _For example, “Lucky” and_ _“Highly Skilled” are too broad, because they could be applied_ _to virtually any roll. Likewise, “Supersonic Flight” and_ _“Invulnerable” imply game-breaking special abilities._

EXAMPLE EXPERIENCES

**Backgrounds:** _Assassin, Blacksmith, Bodyguard, Bounty_ _Hunter, Chef to the Royal Family, Circus Performer,_ _Con Artist, Fallen Monarch, Field Medic, High Priestess,_ _Merchant, Noble, Pirate, Politician, Runaway, Scholar,_ _Sellsword, Soldier, Storyteller, Thief, World Traveler_

**Characteristics:** _Affable, Battle-Hardened, Bookworm,_ _Charming, Cowardly, Friend to All, Helpful, Intimidating_ _{{term:presence|Presence}}, Leader, Lone Wolf, Loyal, Observant, Prankster,_ _Silver Tongue, Sticky Fingers, Stubborn to a Fault, Survivor,_ _Young and Naive_

**Specialties:** _Acrobat, Gambler, Healer, Inventor, Magical_ _Historian, Mapmaker, Master of Disguise, Navigator,_ _Sharpshooter, Survivalist, Swashbuckler, Tactician_

**Skills:** _Animal Whisperer, Barter, Deadly Aim, Fast_ _Learner, Incredible {{term:strength|Strength}}, Liar, Light Feet, Negotiator,_ _Photographic Memory, Quick Hands, Repair, Scavenger,_ _Tracker_

**Phrases:** _Catch Me If You Can, Fake It Till You Make It, First_ _Time’s the Charm, Hold the Line, I Won’t Let You Down,_ _I’ll Catch You, I’ve Got Your Back, {{term:knowledge|Knowledge}} Is Power,_ _Nature’s Friend, Never Again, No One Left Behind, Pick on_ _Someone Your Own Size, The Show Must Go On, This Is Not_ _a Negotiation, Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing_

name: Step 8
text: **Choose Domain Cards.** Your class has access to two of the ten domains. Choose two level one cards from your class’s domains, which are listed in the upper left of your character sheet. You can take one card from each domain or two from a single domain, whichever you prefer.

name: Step 9
text:
**Create Your Connections.** Connections are the relationships between the PCs. To create connections, follow these steps:

- Go around the table and have each player describe their characters to one another—at a minimum, their name, pronouns, character description, experiences, and the answers to their background questions.
- Discuss potential connections between the PCs using the questions included in the “Connections” section of your character guide as inspiration.
- Suggest at least one connection between your character and each other player’s PC. Accept any suggested connections you want to explore, reject any you don’t.

**_Note:_** _A player can reject a suggested connection for any_ _reason, and it’s okay if there isn’t an established connection_ _between every pair of PCs—you can always discover and_ _develop those relationships through play._

name: Domains
text: There are ten Domains, each comprising a collection of cards granting features or special abilities expressing a particular theme. Please note the Daggerheart Core Set includes only the following nine domains: Arcana, Blade, Bone, Codex, Grace, Midnight, Sage, Splendor, and Valor.

name: Class Domains
text:
Each class grants access to two domains:

- **Assassion:** Blade & Midnight
- **Bard:** Codex & Grace
- **Brawler:** Valor & Bone
- **Druid:** Arcana & Sage
- **Guardian:** Blade & Valor
- **Ranger:** Bone & Sage
- **Rogue:** Grace & Midnight
- **Seraph:** Splendor & Valor
- **Sorcerer:** Arcana & Midnight
- **Warlock:** Dread & Grace
- **Warrior:** Blade & Bone
- **Witch:** Dread & Sage
- **Wizard:** Codex & Splendor

PCs acquire two 1st-level {{term:domain-card|domain cards}} at character creation and an additional {{term:domain-card|domain card}} at or below their level each time they level up.

name: Domain Cards
text:
Each {{term:domain-card|domain card}} provides one or more features your PC can utilize during their adventures. Some {{term:domain-card|domain cards}} provide moves you can make, such as a unique attack or a spell. Others offer passive effects, new {{term:downtime|downtime}} or social encounter abilities, or one-time benefits.

### Domain Card Anatomy

Each {{term:domain-card|domain card}} includes six elements:

**Level** The number in the top left of the card indicates the card’s level. You cannot acquire a {{term:domain-card|domain card}} with a level higher than your PC’s.

**Domain** Beneath the card’s level there is a symbol indicating its domain. You can only choose cards from your class’s two domains.

**{{term:recall-cost|Recall Cost}}** The number and lightning bolt in the top right of the card shows its {{term:recall-cost|Recall Cost}}. This is the amount of {{term:stress|Stress}} a player must mark to swap this card from their **{{term:vault|vault}}** with a card from their **{{term:loadout|loadout}}.**

**_Note:_** _A player can swap {{term:domain-card|domain cards}} during {{term:downtime|downtime}}_ _without paying the {{term:domain-card|domain card}}’s {{term:recall-cost|Recall Cost}}._

**Title** The name of the card.

**Type** The card’s **type** is listed in the center above the title. There are three types of {{term:domain-card|domain cards}}: **abilities, spells,** and **grimoires.** Abilities are typically non-magical in nature, while spells are magical. Grimoires are unique to the Codex domain and grant access to a collection of less potent spells. Some game mechanics only apply to certain types of cards.

**Feature** The text on the bottom half of the card describes its feature(s), including any special rules you need to follow when you use that card.

### Loadout & Vault

Your **{{term:loadout|loadout}}** is the set of acquired cards whose effects your PC can use during play. You can have up to five {{term:domain-card|domain cards}} in your {{term:loadout|loadout}} at one time. Once you’ve acquired six or more {{term:domain-card|domain cards}}, you must choose five to keep in your {{term:loadout|loadout}}; the rest are considered to be in your **{{term:vault|vault}}.** Vault cards are inactive and do not influence play

**_Note:_** _Your subclass, ancestry, and community cards don’t_ _contribute to your {{term:loadout|loadout}} maximum and are always active_ _and available._

At the start of a rest, before using {{term:downtime|downtime moves}}, you can freely move cards between your {{term:loadout|loadout}} and your {{term:vault|vault}}, so long as your {{term:loadout|loadout}} doesn’t exceed its five-card maximum.

To move a card from your {{term:vault|vault}} to your {{term:loadout|loadout}} at any other time, you must mark a number of {{term:stress|Stress}} equal to the vaulted card’s **{{term:recall-cost|Recall Cost}}** (located in the top right of the card next to the lightning bolt symbol). If your {{term:loadout|loadout}} is already full, you must also move a card from your {{term:loadout|loadout}} to your {{term:vault|vault}} to make space, though you can do this at no cost.

When you gain a new {{term:domain-card|domain card}} at level-up, you can immediately move it into your {{term:loadout|loadout}} for free. If your {{term:loadout|loadout}} is already full, you must also move a card from your {{term:loadout|loadout}} to your {{term:vault|vault}} to make space.

### Usage Limits

If a {{term:domain-card|domain card}} restricts how often it can be used, you can track such limits with whatever method you prefer, such as turning the card sideways, flipping it facedown, or using tokens.

**_Note:_** _if an effect or ability gives you a number of uses equal_ _to a trait with a modifier of +0 or less, it grants you 0 uses._

name: Classes
text:
A **class** is a role-based archetype that determines a PC’s:

- **Access to Domains:** Each class grants access to two domains; players choose cards from these domains during character creation and when leveling up.
- **Starting {{term:evasion|Evasion}} and {{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} ({{term:hit-points|HP}})**
- **Starting Items**
- **Class Feature(s)**
- **Class {{term:hope|Hope}} Feature,** a class feature that costs 3 {{term:hope|Hope}} to activate.

Please note that the Daggerheart Core Set includes only the following nine classes: Bard, Druid, Guardian, Ranger, Rogue, Seraph, Sorcerer, Warrior, and Wizard.

name: Subclasses
text:
Each class is divided into two **subclasses,** each of which further defines and highlights one aspect of its class archetype. Your chosen subclass can grant the following:

- {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast Trait}}: This is the trait used on all Spellcast rolls.
- Foundation Feature: This is a unique starting feature that establishes the identity and strengths of the subclass. You gain your chosen subclass's Foundation at character creation.
- Specialization Feature: This is an advanced feature that can be gained on level up. For some subclasses, the specialization feature grants a new ability; for others, it expands or enhances a feature you already acquired through a class or subclass.
- Mastery Feature: The mastery feature is a subclass’s most powerful feature, which can be gained at higher levels. For some subclasses, the mastery feature unlocks an extraordinary new ability; for others, it’s the impressive culmination of their subclass’s core feature.

When you acquire a Foundation, Specialization, or Mastery, take its card for use as a reference during play.

name: Martial Stances
text:
When you choose the Martial Artist subclass, take the Martial Stances sheet to track which stances your character knows. You can also track which stance you have active and your current Focus.

### Stances

Stances are special body positionings that enable Martial Artists to attack, react, or defend in combat. Each stance grants your character a different ability, bonus, or feature while active.

You choose two stances from Tier 1 when you first take the Martial Artist’s subclass foundation card. Mark the circle next to each to indicate that your character knows and has access to them. Mark a new stance from your {{term:tier|tier}} or below each time you gain a level.

### Focus

Focus represents your character’s poise, clarity, and control. Once per rest during a moment of calm, you can clear your mind and refocus your martial instincts. Clear your Focus track, then roll a number of **d6s** equal to your {{term:instinct|Instinct}} and gain Focus equal to the highest result rolled. You can hold a maximum of 6 Focus.

### Shifting Into Stances

You can **spend a Focus** to shift into a martial stance and gain its effects. You can shift only into stances you’ve marked as known. When you shift into a stance, it’s considered your active stance until you drop out of it.

You can’t shift into or have more than one active stance at a time. Until you shift into a stance, you are not considered to be in a stance or to have an active stance.

### Dropping Out of Stances

If you are already in a stance when you shift into a different stance, you automatically drop out of the previously active stance. You also drop out of your active stance when you take {{term:damage-thresholds|Severe damage}} or mark your last {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}}. Otherwise, you drop out of your active stance at the end of the scene. When you drop out of a stance, you lose any ongoing benefits it provides.

### Stance Features

The following section lists all martial stances by {{term:tier|tier}}.

TIER 1

**_Favored:_** Gain a bonus to damage rolls equal to a trait of your choice.

**_Invigorating:_** On a successful attack, roll a **d4**. On a result of 4, gain a Focus.

**_Quick:_** When you make an attack, you can **spend a Focus** or **mark a {{term:stress|Stress}}** to target another creature within range with that attack.

**_Reliable:_** Gain a +1 bonus to your attack rolls.

TIER 2

**_Aggressive:_** Gain a −1 penalty to your {{term:evasion|Evasion}}. On a successful attack, roll an additional damage die and discard the lowest result.

**_Anchored:_** Gain a +2 bonus to your {{term:damage-thresholds|damage thresholds}}. While in this stance, you can’t be moved against your will.

**_Defensive:_** Attack rolls targeting you from within {{term:melee|Melee range}} have {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} unless the attacker marks a {{term:stress|Stress}} to negate the {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}}.

**_Otherworldly:_** On a successful attack, you can deal physical or magic damage.

TIER 3

**_Grappling:_** On a successful attack within {{term:melee|Melee range}}, you can **spend a Focus** or **mark a {{term:stress|Stress}}** to {{term:temporary|temporarily}} _{{term:restrained|Restrain}}_ the target or throw the target up to {{term:close|Close range}}.

**_Scary:_** On a successful attack, the target must mark a {{term:stress|Stress}}.

**_Stable:_** You can **spend a Focus** instead of an {{term:armor-slot|Armor Slot}} to reduce damage.

**_Vigilant:_** When you are targeted by an attack, you can **mark** **a {{term:stress|Stress}}** to gain a **d6** bonus to your {{term:evasion|Evasion}} against the attack.

TIER 4

**_Crushing:_** When you deal {{term:damage-thresholds|Severe damage}}, you can **spend a** **{{term:hope|Hope}}** to force the target to mark an additional {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}}.

**_Exacting:_** When you roll a 1 on a damage die, you can treat it as the highest value on the die instead.

**_Honed:_** **Spend a Focus** before you make an attack roll to gain a +1 bonus to your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} for that attack.

**_Isolating:_** Gain {{term:advantage|advantage}} on attack rolls when there are no other creatures within {{term:very-close|Very Close range}} of you or your target.

name: Beastform Options
text:
When you use your “Beastform” feature, choose a creature category of your {{term:tier|tier}} or lower. At the GM’s discretion, you can describe yourself transforming into any animal that reasonably fits into that category.

Beastform categories are divided by {{term:tier|tier}}. Each entry includes the following details:

- **Creature Category:** Each category’s name describes the common role or behavior of creatures in that category (such as Agile Scout). This name is followed by a few examples of animals that fit in that category (in this example, fox, mouse, and weasel).
- **Character Trait:** While transformed, you gain a bonus to the listed trait. For example, while transformed into an Agile Scout, you gain a +1 bonus to your {{term:agility|Agility}}. When this form drops, you lose this bonus.
- **Attack Rolls:** When you make an attack while transformed, you use the creature’s listed range, trait, and damage dice, but you use your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}}. For example, as an Agile Scout, you can attack a target within {{term:melee|Melee range}} using your {{term:agility|Agility}}. On a success, you deal d4 physical damage using your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}}.
- **{{term:evasion|Evasion}}:** While transformed, you add the creature’s {{term:evasion|Evasion}} bonus to your normal {{term:evasion|Evasion}}. For example, if your {{term:evasion|Evasion}} is usually 8 and your Beastform says “{{term:evasion|Evasion}} +2,” your {{term:evasion|Evasion}} becomes 10 while you’re in that form.
- **Advantages:** Your form makes you especially suited to certain actions. When you make an action or {{term:reaction-roll|reaction roll}} related to one of the verbs listed for that creature category, you gain {{term:advantage|advantage}} on that roll. For example, an Agile Scout gains {{term:advantage|advantage}} on rolls made to sneak around, search for objects or creatures, and related activities.
- **Features:** Each form includes unique features. For example, an Agile Scout excels at silent, dexterous movement—but they’re also fragile, making you more likely to drop out of Beastform.

name: Ranger Companion
text:
When you choose the Beastbound Ranger subclass, take a companion sheet. This sheet is for tracking important information about your character’s companion and can be tucked beneath the right side of your character sheet for ease of viewing.

STEP 1: NAME YOUR COMPANION Work with the GM to decide what kind of animal you have as your companion. Give them a name and add a picture of them to the companion sheet.

STEP 2: WRITE THEIR EVASION Fill in their {{term:evasion|Evasion}}, which starts at 10.

STEP 3: CHOOSE THEIR COMPANION EXPERIENCE Create two {{term:experience|Experiences}} for your companion based on their training and the history you have together.

Start with +2 in both {{term:experience|Experiences}}. Whenever you gain a new {{term:experience|Experience}}, your companion also gains one. All new {{term:experience|Experiences}} start at +2.

**Example Companion {{term:experience|Experiences}}**

_Bold Distraction, Expert Climber, Fetch, Friendly, Guardian_ _of the Forest, Horrifying, Intimidating, Loyal Until the_ _End, Navigation, Nimble, Nobody Left Behind, On High_ _Alert, Protective, Royal Companion, Scout, Service Animal,_ _Trusted Mount, Vigilant, We Always Find Them, You Can’t_ _Hit What You Can’t Find_

STEP 4: CHOOSE THEIR ATTACK AND RECORD DAMAGE DIE Finally, describe your companion’s method of dealing damage (their standard attack) and record it in the “Attack & Damage” section. At level 1, your companion’s damage die is a d6 and their range is Melee. Choose whether they deal physical or magic damage.

name: Working with Your Companion
text:
The following sections will run you through the basics of working with your companion.

USING SPELLCAST ROLLS, HOPE, AND EXPERIENCES Make a {{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Roll}} to connect with your companion and command them to take action. Spend a {{term:hope|Hope}} to add an applicable Companion {{term:experience|Experience}} to the roll. On a success with {{term:hope|Hope}}, if your next action builds on their success, you gain {{term:advantage|advantage}} on the roll.

ATTACKING WITH YOUR COMPANION When you command your companion to attack, they gain any benefits that would normally only apply to you (such as the effects of “Ranger’s Focus”). On a success, their damage roll uses your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} and their damage die.

TAKING DAMAGE AS STRESS

- When your companion would take any amount of damage, they mark a {{term:stress|Stress}}. When they mark their last {{term:stress|Stress}}, they drop out of the scene (by hiding, fleeing, or a similar action). They remain unavailable until the start of your next {{term:long-rest|long rest}}, where they return with 1 {{term:stress|Stress}} cleared.
- When you choose a {{term:downtime|downtime move}} that clears {{term:stress|Stress}} on yourself, your companion clears an equal number of {{term:stress|Stress}}.

name: Leveling Up Your Companion
text:
When your character levels up, choose one available option for your companion from the following list and mark it on your sheet:

- **_Intelligent:_** Your companion gains a permanent +1 bonus to a Companion {{term:experience|Experience}} of your choice.
- **_Light in the Dark:_** Use this as an additional {{term:hope|Hope}} slot your character can mark.
- **_Creature Comfort:_** Once per rest, when you take time during a quiet moment to give your companion love and attention, you can gain a {{term:hope|Hope}} or you can both clear a {{term:stress|Stress}}.
- **_Armored:_** When your companion takes damage, you can **mark one of your {{term:armor-slot|Armor Slots}}** instead of marking one of their {{term:stress|Stress}}.
- **_Vicious:_** Increase your companion’s damage dice or range by one step (d6 to d8, Close to Far, etc.).
- **_Resilient:_** Your companion gains an additional {{term:stress|Stress}} slot.
- **_Bonded:_** When you mark your last {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}}, your companion rushes to your side to comfort you. Roll a number of **d6s** equal to the unmarked {{term:stress|Stress}} slots they have and mark them. If any roll a 6, your companion helps you up. Clear your last {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}} and return to the scene.
- **_Aware:_** Your companion gains a permanent +2 bonus to their {{term:evasion|Evasion}}.

name: Ancestries
text:
**Ancestries** represent your character’s lineage, which affects their physical appearance and access to certain special abilities. The following section describes each ancestry in Daggerheart and the characteristics generally shared by members of that ancestry, however, each player decides how much their character aligns with the “standard” or “average” expression of their ancestry.

In Daggerheart, the term “people” is used to refer to all ancestries, as individuals from all lineages possess unique characteristics and cultures, as well as personhood.

Some ancestries are described using the term “humanoid.” This does not imply any genetic relation to “humans,” which is a distinct ancestry within Daggerheart. Instead, it refers to the set of physical characteristics humans will recognize from their own anatomy, such as bipedal movement, upright posture, facial layout, and more. These traits vary by ancestry and individual, though “humanoid” should still provide a useful frame of reference.

The Daggerheart Core Set includes only the following ancestries: Clank, Drakona, Dwarf, Elf, Faerie, Faun, Firbolg, Fungril, Galapa, Giant, Goblin, Halfling, Human, Infernis, Katari, Orc, Ribbet, Simiah, and Mixed Ancestry.

name: Ancestry Features
text:
Each ancestry grants two **ancestry features.** While some features (such as the ability to fly) are implicitly tied to an ancestry’s anatomy, players determine their characters’ physical form. Work with the GM to re-flavor any implied traits that don’t align with your character concept.

If you’d like to make a character who combines more than one ancestry, see “Mixed Ancestry.”

name: Elemental Kin
text:
Elemental kin are humanoid mortals descended from powerful supernatural entities known as elementals—embodiments of the fundamental forces that shape the Mortal Realm (such as earth, air, fire, and water). These “kin” manifest forces differently, with some appearing more or less humanoid than others, but they all have a lineage that grants them unique ways to harness and influence their elemental heritage.

At birth, elemental kin closely resemble the element they embody, then become increasingly humanoid as they mature through early childhood. As they grow, their appearance manifests unique characteristics that identify them as elemental kin, such as crystal formations across a stonekin’s shoulders or a skykin’s ever-present breeze tousling their hair. While adult elemental kin are predominantly flesh and blood, small portions of their bodies momentarily shift into an elemental state in times of great emotion. Elemental kin with limb differences, or who lost a limb at some point in their life, can also manipulate a small amount of their element to help them accomplish a variety of tasks.

Some elemental kins’ physical characteristics are passed down through families, such as one family of earthkin bearing shifting skin with the texture of sand, while another bears marble patterns. Additionally, families often develop their own unique communication styles that use their elemental influence. For example, emberkin might express excitement with flares of fire from their eyes, while tidekin might use currents of color over their bodies to communicate subtle messages.

Though their lifespans vary, all elemental kin return to their element upon their death.

name: Mixed Ancestry
text:
Families within the world of Daggerheart are as unique as the peoples and cultures that inhabit it. Anyone’s appearance and abilities can be shaped by blood, magic, proximity, or a variety of other factors.

If you decide that your character is a descendant of multiple ancestries and you want to mechanically represent that in the game, use the steps below:

1. **Determine Ancestry Combination** When you choose an ancestry at character creation, write down how your character identifies themself in the Heritage section of your character sheet. For example, if your character is descended from both goblins and orcs, you could use a hybridized term, such as “goblin-orc,” to describe your ancestry, list only the ancestry you more closely identify with (e.g., just “goblin” or just “orc”), or invent a new term, such as “toothling.”
2. **Choose Ancestry Features** Work with your GM to choose two features from the ancestries in your character’s lineage. You must choose the first feature from one ancestry and the second from another. Write both down on a notecard you can keep with your other cards or next to your character sheet.

_For example, if you are making a goblin-orc, you might take_ _the “Surefooted” and “Tusks” features or the “Sturdy” and_ _“Danger Sense” features. You can’t take both the “Surefooted”_ _and “Sturdy” features, because these are both the first_ _features listed on their respective ancestry cards._

Your character's heritage might include more than two ancestries, but you still only choose features from two. You can represent additional ancestries through their appearance or backstory.

name: Communities
text:
Communities represent a key aspect of the **culture, class,** or **environment of origin** that has had the most influence over your character’s upbringing.

Your character’s community grants them a **community** **feature.** Each community card also lists six adjectives you can use as inspiration to create your character’s personality, their relationship to their peers, their attitude toward their upbringing, or the demeanor with which they interact with the rest of the party. Please note the Daggerheart Core Set includes only the following communities: Highborne, Loreborne, Orderborne, Ridgeborne, Seaborne, Slyborne, Underborne, Wanderborne, Wildborne.

name: Transformations
text:
Transformations represent a fundamental shift in your character and how they interact with the world. These are optional aspects of a character’s identity that the GM can give out during a campaign as part of the narrative or, at their discretion, present as an option during character creation.

Transformations provide both a mechanical benefit and a drawback. Taking a transformation card requires you to buy into the concept of the exchange, taking on the {{term:burden|burden}} to reap the benefit. Because of this, we recommend that players remind GMs of their transformations' negative effects whenever they’re relevant to help fulfill and reinforce the fiction of the transformation.

Transformation cards do not count toward your {{term:loadout|loadout}} maximum. When your character gains a transformation, add the card to your {{term:loadout|loadout}} as if it were part of your character’s heritage. Consider how this transformation changes your character physically and psychologically—if you need inspiration, each transformation includes questions to help you.

If there are details you’d like to incorporate into your character that go beyond the features on a transformation card, work with your GM to explore how they might manifest in your campaign’s narrative.

A PC can't have more than one transformation.

name: Granting Transformations
text:
GMs should discuss transformations with their players before incorporating them into their campaigns. A transformation can deeply impact a PC’s narrative journey, so it’s best to ensure this aspect of the game supports the story your players want to tell and is something they’ll enjoy.

Some of the transformations presented here are easy to introduce during a campaign as a narrative development. For example, the vampire or werewolf transformation could be gained when the campaign’s major villain targets a PC with a significant attack. A PC who gains the reanimated or ghost transformation might have died in a place of great magic or made a story-altering bargain in exchange for their resurrection. These transformations can also be part of character creation. Maybe a PC was born a werewolf and seeks to control this aspect of their lineage, or a PC is a long-dead ghost who haunts the party to protect the living.

Some transformations are more likely to be taken at character creation, such as the shapeshifter or demigod. However, they can still be introduced as a character twist during a campaign. It’s ultimately up to you which transformations are available at character creation and how they become available throughout play—decide what works best for you, your players, and the story you’re telling together.

name: Flow of the Game
text: Daggerheart is a conversation. The GM describes fictional scenarios involving the PCs, and the players take turns describing how their characters react. The goal of every person at the table is to build upon everyone else’s ideas and collaboratively tell a satisfying story. The system facilitates this collaborative process by providing structure to the conversation and mechanics for resolving moments of tension where fate or fortune determine the outcome of events.

name: Player Principles & Best Practices
text: To get the most out of Daggerheart, we recommend players keep the following principles and practices in mind throughout each session:

name: Principles
text:
- Be a fan of your character and their journey.
- Spotlight your friends.
- Address the characters and address the players.
- Build the world together.
- Play to find out what happens.
- Hold on gently.

name: Best Practices
text:
- Embrace danger.
- Use your resources.
- Tell the story.
- Discover your character.

_For more information, see the Daggerheart Core Rulebook,_ _pages 9 and 108._

name: Core Gameplay Loop
text: The **core gameplay loop** is the procedure that drives every scene, both in and out of combat:

name: Step 1 Set the Scene
text: The GM describes a scenario, establishing the PCs’ surroundings and any dangers, NPCs, or other important details the characters would notice.

name: Step 2 Ask and Answer Questions
text: The players ask clarifying questions to explore the scene more deeply and gather information that could inform their characters’ actions. The GM responds to these questions by giving the players information their characters could easily obtain, or by asking questions of their own to the players. The players also respond to any questions the GM poses to them. In this way, the table builds out the fiction collaboratively.

name: Step 3 Build on the Fiction
text: As the scene develops, the players find opportunities to take action—problems to solve, obstacles to overcome, mysteries to investigate, and so on. The players describe how their characters proceed; if their proposed actions carry no chance of failure (or if failure would be boring), they automatically succeed. But if the outcome of their action is unknown, the GM calls for an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}. Either way, the table works the outcome into the story and moves the fiction forward, narrating how the PC’s actions have changed things.

name: Step 4 Go Back to Step 1
text: The process repeats from the beginning, with the GM relaying any updated details or material changes to the players. This process continues until the end of the scene is triggered by a mechanic or arrives organically.

name: The Spotlight
text:
The **{{term:spotlight|spotlight}}** is a symbol that represents the table’s attention—and therefore the immediate focus of both the narrative and the game mechanics. Any time a character or player becomes the focus of a scene, they “are in the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}” or “have the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}.”

The {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} moves around the table organically as scenes unfold unless a mechanical trigger determines where the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} goes next. For example, when a player fails an {{term:action-roll|action roll}} or rolls with {{term:fear|Fear}}, the mechanics prompt the GM to seize the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} and make a GM move.

name: Turn Order & Action Economy
text:
Daggerheart’s turns don’t follow a traditional, rigid format: there is no explicit initiative mechanic and characters don’t have a set number of actions they can take or things they can do before the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} passes to someone else. A player with the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} describes what their character does, and the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} swings to one of the following:

- Whomever or whatever a triggered mechanic puts it on
- Whomever or whatever the fiction would naturally focus on next
- A character who hasn't had the focus in a while

**Optional: Spotlight Tracker Tool**

If your group prefers a more traditional action economy, you can use tokens to track how many times a player has had the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}: At the start of a session or scene, each player adds a certain number of tokens (we recommend 3) to their character sheet and removes a token each time they take an action. If the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} would swing to someone without any tokens, it swings to someone else instead. Once every player has used all their available tokens, players refill their character sheet with the same number of tokens as before, then continue playing.

name: Making Moves & Taking Action
text: Any time a character does something to advance the story, such as speaking with another character, interacting with the environment, making an attack, casting a spell, or using a class feature, they are making a move.

name: Action Rolls
text: Any move where success would be trivial or failure would be boring automatically succeeds, but any move that’s difficult to accomplish or risky to attempt triggers an **{{term:action-roll|action roll}}.**

name: Overview
text:
All {{term:action-roll|action rolls}} require a pair of d12s called **{{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}}.** These are two visually distinct twelve-sided dice, with one die representing {{term:hope|Hope}} and the other representing {{term:fear|Fear}}.

To make an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, you roll the {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}}, sum the results, apply any relevant modifiers, and compare the total to a {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} number to determine the outcome:

- **Success with {{term:hope|Hope}}:** If your total meets or beats the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} AND your {{term:duality-dice|Hope Die}} shows a higher result than your {{term:duality-dice|Fear Die}}, you rolled a “Success with {{term:hope|Hope}}.” You succeed and gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}, and the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} stays with the players.
- **Success with {{term:fear|Fear}}:** If your total meets or beats the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} AND your {{term:duality-dice|Fear Die}} shows a higher result than your {{term:duality-dice|Hope Die}}, you rolled a “Success with {{term:fear|Fear}}.” You succeed with a cost or complication, but the GM gains a {{term:fear|Fear}}, then takes the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}.
- **Failure with {{term:hope|Hope}}:** If your total is less than the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} AND your {{term:duality-dice|Hope Die}} shows a higher result than your {{term:duality-dice|Fear Die}}, you rolled a “Failure with {{term:hope|Hope}}.” You fail with a minor consequence and gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}, then the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} swings to the GM.
- **Failure with {{term:fear|Fear}}:** If your total is less than the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} AND your {{term:duality-dice|Fear Die}} shows a higher result than your {{term:duality-dice|Hope Die}}, you rolled a “Failure with {{term:fear|Fear}}.” You fail with a major consequence and the GM gains a {{term:fear|Fear}}, then the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} swings to the GM.
- **{{term:critical-success|Critical Success}}:** If the {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}} show matching results, you rolled a “{{term:critical-success|Critical Success}}” (“Crit”). You automatically succeed with a bonus, gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}, and clear a {{term:stress|Stress}}. If this was an attack roll, you deal critical damage.

**_Note:_** _A {{term:critical-success|Critical Success}} counts as a roll “with {{term:hope|Hope}}.”_

After resolving the {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, the table works together to weave the outcome into the narrative and play continues.

### Failing Forward

In Daggerheart, every time you roll the dice, the scene changes in some way. There is no such thing as a roll where “nothing happens,” because the fiction constantly evolves based on the successes and failures of the characters.

name: Procedure
text:
The following steps describe in more detail the procedure that all {{term:action-roll|action rolls}} utilize:

**STEP 1:** PICK AN APPROPRIATE TRAIT

Some actions and effects specify in their description which trait applies to the roll; otherwise, the GM tells the acting player which character trait best applies to the action being attempted. If more than one trait could apply to the roll, the GM chooses or lets the acting player decide.

**STEP 2:** DETERMINE THE DIFFICULTY

Some actions and features say in their description what the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} is. Otherwise, the GM determines the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} based on the scenario. The GM can choose whether to share the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} with the table. In either case, the GM should communicate the potential consequences of failure to the acting player.

**STEP 3:** APPLY EXTRA DICE AND MODIFIERS

The acting player decides whether to Utilize an {{term:experience|Experience}} or activate other effects, then, if applicable, adds the appropriate tokens and dice (such as {{term:advantage|advantage}} or Rally dice) to their dice pool.

**_Note:_** _Unless an action, ability, or feature specifically allows_ _for it, a player must declare the use of any {{term:experience|Experiences}}, extra_ _dice, or other modifiers before they roll._

**STEP 4:** ROLL THE DICE

The acting player rolls their entire dice pool and announces the results in the format of “[total result] with [{{term:hope|Hope}}/{{term:fear|Fear}}]”—or “{{term:critical-success|Critical Success}}!” in the case of matching {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}}.

_Example: A player is making an {{term:action-roll|action roll}} with a +1 in the_ _relevant trait and no other modifiers; they roll the Duality_ _Dice and get a result of 5 on their {{term:duality-dice|Hope Die}} and 7 on their_ _{{term:duality-dice|Fear Die}}, then announce “I rolled a 13 with {{term:fear|Fear}}!”_

**STEP 5:** RESOLVE THE OUTCOME

The active player and the GM work together, along with the suggestions and support of the rest of the table, to resolve the outcome of the action.

name: GM Moves and Adversary Actions
text:
GMs also make moves. They should consider making a move when a player does one of the following things:

- Rolls with {{term:fear|Fear}} on an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}.
- Fails an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}.
- Does something that would have consequences.
- Gives them a golden opportunity.
- Looks to them for what happens next.

After the GM turn is done, the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} goes back to the PCs.

Many adversaries and environments have **{{term:fear|Fear}} Features**, especially powerful or consequential moves that the GM must spend {{term:fear|Fear}} to activate.

**_Note:_** _This {{term:fear|Fear}} is in addition to any {{term:fear|Fear}} the GM has_ _previously spent to seize the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} or activate another_ _action or ability._

name: Adversary Actions
text:
When play passes to the GM, the GM can make a GM move to {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} an adversary. When an adversary takes the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}, they do one of the following:

- Move within {{term:close|Close range}} and make a standard attack
- Move within {{term:close|Close range}} and use an adversary action
- Clear a {{term:temporary|temporary}} condition
- Sprint within Far or {{term:very-far|Very Far range}} on the battlefield
- Anything else the fiction demands or the GM deems appropriate

The GM can spend additional {{term:fear|Fear}} to {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} additional adversaries. Once the GM has finished, the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} swings back to the PCs.

name: Special Rolls
text:
Some rolls have unique specifications or otherwise modify the {{term:action-roll|action roll}} procedure: trait rolls, {{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Rolls}}, attack rolls, and damage rolls. Unless otherwise noted, you can apply any bonus, modifier, or effect to a special roll as if it were a standard {{term:action-roll|action roll}}.

### Trait Rolls

An {{term:action-roll|action roll}} that specifies which character trait applies to it is called a **trait roll.** In the text of a feature or effect, a trait roll is referenced with the format “[Trait] Roll ({{term:difficulty|Difficulty}})” (e.g., “{{term:agility|Agility}} Roll (12)”). If the text of an effect doesn’t specify a trait roll’s {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}}, the GM sets the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} based on the circumstances.

Features and effects that affect a trait roll also affect any {{term:action-roll|action roll}} that uses the same trait, including attack rolls, {{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Rolls}}, and standard {{term:action-roll|action rolls}}.

**Example:** The katari’s ancestry feature “Feline Instincts,” which allows the katari to reroll an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll, can be used on a standard {{term:action-roll|action roll}} using {{term:agility|Agility}} to traverse dangerous terrain or on an attack roll made with a weapon that uses {{term:agility|Agility}}.

### Spellcast Rolls

**{{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Rolls}}** are trait rolls that require you to use your {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast trait}}. Your {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast trait}}, if you have one, is determined by your subclass.

{{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Rolls}} are only made when a character uses a feature that requires one. A successful {{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Roll}} activates the effect as described by the feature.

**_Notes:_**

_A {{term:spellcast-roll|Spellcast Roll}} that can damage a target is also considered_ _an attack roll._

_When you cast a spell, the text tells you when the effect ends._ _The GM can spend a {{term:fear|Fear}} to end a {{term:temporary|temporary}} effect. If your_ _spell doesn’t specify when it ends, it ends when you choose or_ _at a natural moment of the story. You can choose to end your_ _spell early._

_You can cast and maintain the effects of more than one spell_ _at the same time._

### Reaction Rolls

A **{{term:reaction-roll|reaction roll}}** is made in response to an attack or a hazard, representing a character’s attempt to avoid or withstand an imminent effect.

Reaction rolls work like {{term:action-roll|action rolls}}, except they don’t generate {{term:hope|Hope}} or {{term:fear|Fear}}, don’t trigger additional GM moves, and other characters can’t aid you with {{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}}.

If you critically succeed on a {{term:reaction-roll|reaction roll}}, you don’t clear a {{term:stress|Stress}} or gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}, but you do ignore any effects that would have impacted you on a success, such as taking damage or marking {{term:stress|Stress}}.

### Group Action Rolls

When multiple PCs take action together, the party chooses one PC to **lead the action.** Each other player then describes how their character collaborates on the task. The leader makes an {{term:action-roll|action roll}} as usual, while the other players make {{term:reaction-roll|reaction rolls}} using whichever traits they and the GM decide fit best.

The lead character gains a +1 bonus to their lead {{term:action-roll|action roll}} for each of these {{term:reaction-roll|reaction rolls}} that succeeded and a −1 penalty for each these {{term:reaction-roll|reaction rolls}} that failed.

### Tag Team Rolls

Each player can, once per session, initiate a **{{term:tag-team-roll|Tag Team Roll}}** between their character and another PC by spending 3 {{term:hope|Hope}}. The players work with one another to describe how they combine their actions in a unique and exciting way. Both players make separate {{term:action-roll|action rolls}}; before resolving the roll’s outcome, choose one of the rolls to apply to both actions. On a roll with {{term:hope|Hope}}, all PCs involved gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}. On a roll with {{term:fear|Fear}}, the GM gains a {{term:fear|Fear}} token for each PC involved.

On a successful Tag Team attack roll, both players roll damage and add the totals together to determine the damage dealt, which is then treated as if it came from a single source. If the attacks deal different types of damage, the players choose which type to deal.

**_Notes:_**

_A {{term:tag-team-roll|Tag Team Roll}} counts as a single {{term:action-roll|action roll}} for the_ _purposes of any {{term:countdown|countdowns}} or features that track action_ _rolls._

_Though each player may only initiate one {{term:tag-team-roll|Tag Team Roll}} per_ _session, one PC can be involved in multiple {{term:tag-team-roll|Tag Team Rolls}}._

name: Advantage & Disadvantage
text:
Some features and effects let you roll with {{term:advantage|advantage}} or {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} on an action or {{term:reaction-roll|reaction roll}}:

- **{{term:advantage|Advantage}}** represents an opportunity that you seize to increase your chances of success. When you roll with {{term:advantage|advantage}}, you roll a d6 {{term:advantage|advantage}} die and add its result to your total.
- **{{term:disadvantage|Disadvantage}}** represents an additional difficulty, hardship, or challenge you face when attempting an action. When you roll with {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}}, you roll a d6 {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} die and subtract its result from your total.

{{term:advantage|Advantage}} or {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} can be granted or imposed by mechanical triggers or at the GM’s discretion.

Regardless of how many sources grant them {{term:advantage|advantage}} or {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}}, a player never rolls more than one {{term:advantage|advantage}} or {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} die on the same roll.

Likewise, advantages and disadvantages cancel one another, one for one, when they would apply to the same roll. Therefore, a player never makes a roll with both an {{term:advantage|advantage}} die and a {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} die.

**_For example:_** _If a player would gain {{term:advantage|advantage}} on an action_ _from three different sources and {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}} from one, they_ _would still only gain one {{term:advantage|advantage}} die on the roll._

There is one exception to this general rule. When a player uses {{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}}, they roll their own {{term:advantage|advantage}} die and apply it to an ally’s {{term:action-roll|action roll}}. Any number of players can {{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}} on the same {{term:action-roll|action roll}}. If multiple {{term:advantage|advantage}} dice apply to the same {{term:action-roll|action roll}} due to one or more players using {{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}}, the player making the {{term:action-roll|action roll}} adds only the highest result of all {{term:advantage|advantage}} dice rolled (including their own) and ignores the rest.

**_For example:_** _Anne makes an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll with {{term:advantage|advantage}},_ _and her allies Bo and Cameron both spend a {{term:hope|Hope}} to Help_ _an Ally. All three players roll their own d6 {{term:advantage|advantage}} die, but_ _Anne only adds the highest result to her total. So if Anne has_ _+1 in {{term:agility|Agility}} and rolls a 13 with {{term:hope|Hope}} on her {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}},_ _plus a 2 on her {{term:advantage|advantage}} die, but Bo and Cameron rolled a 3_ _and 4 on their {{term:advantage|advantage}} dice, then Anne’s total result would_ _be an 18 with {{term:hope|Hope}} (13 + 1 + 4)._

name: Hope & Fear
text:
**{{term:hope|Hope}}** and **{{term:fear|Fear}}** are metacurrencies representing the cosmic forces that shape the events of your table’s story. {{term:hope|Hope}} powers PC abilities and features, while {{term:fear|Fear}} powers the abilities of the GM and the adversaries and environments they control.

### Hope

Every PC starts with 2 {{term:hope|Hope}} at character creation and gains more throughout play. A PC can have a maximum of 6 {{term:hope|Hope}} at one time, and {{term:hope|Hope}} carries over between sessions.

Players can spend {{term:hope|Hope}} to:

- **{{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}}** When you {{term:help-an-ally|Help an Ally}} who is making an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, describe how you do so and roll an {{term:advantage|advantage}} die. Multiple players can spend {{term:hope|Hope}} to help the same acting player, but that player only adds the highest result to their final total.
- **Utilize an {{term:experience|Experience}}** When you Utilize an {{term:experience|Experience}} on a relevant roll, add its modifier to the result. You can spend multiple {{term:hope|Hope}} to utilize multiple {{term:experience|Experiences}}.
- **Initiate a {{term:tag-team-roll|Tag Team Roll}}** Spend 3 {{term:hope|Hope}} to initiate a Tag Team roll, combining the actions of two PCs into one impressive act of synergy. When you make a Tag Team roll, both players roll their {{term:action-roll|action rolls}} and then choose which set of results to apply to the outcome.
- **Activate a {{term:hope|Hope}} Feature** A {{term:hope|Hope}} Feature is any effect that allows (or requires) you to spend a specified amount of {{term:hope|Hope}} to activate it. **Class** **{{term:hope|Hope}} features** are class-specific features, detailed on your character sheet, that cost 3 {{term:hope|Hope}} to activate.

**_Note:_** _When using a {{term:hope|Hope}} Feature, if you rolled with {{term:hope|Hope}}_ _for that action, the {{term:hope|Hope}} you gain from that roll can be spent_ _on that feature (or toward it, if it requires spending multiple_ _{{term:hope|Hope}})._

### Fear

The GM gains {{term:fear|Fear}} whenever a player rolls with {{term:fear|Fear}} and can spend {{term:fear|Fear}} at any time to make or enhance a GM move or to use a {{term:fear|Fear}} Feature. The GM can have up to 12 {{term:fear|Fear}} at one time. {{term:fear|Fear}} carries over between sessions.

name: Combat
text: Though Daggerheart relies on the same flow of collaborative storytelling in and out of combat, physical conflicts rely more heavily on several key mechanics related to attacking, maneuvering, and taking damage.

name: Evasion
text:
**{{term:evasion|Evasion}}** represents a character’s ability to avoid attacks and other unwanted effects. Any roll made against a PC has a {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} equal to the target’s {{term:evasion|Evasion}}. A PC’s base {{term:evasion|Evasion}} is determined by their class, but can be modified by {{term:domain-card|domain cards}}, equipment, conditions, and other effects.

**_Note:_** _attacks rolled against adversaries use the target’s_ _{{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} instead of {{term:evasion|Evasion}}._

name: Hit Points & Damage Thresholds
text:
**{{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} ({{term:hit-points|HP}})** represent a character’s ability to withstand physical injury. When a character takes damage, they mark 1 to 3 {{term:hit-points|HP}}, based on their **{{term:damage-thresholds|damage thresholds}}:**

- If the final damage is at or above the character’s {{term:damage-thresholds|Severe damage}} threshold, they mark 3 {{term:hit-points|HP}}.
- If the final damage is at or above the character’s {{term:damage-thresholds|Major damage}} threshold but below their {{term:damage-thresholds|Severe damage}} threshold, they mark 2 {{term:hit-points|HP}}.
- If the final damage is below the character’s {{term:damage-thresholds|Major damage}} threshold, they mark 1 {{term:hit-points|HP}}.
- If {{term:incoming-damage|incoming damage}} is ever reduced to 0 or less, no {{term:hit-points|HP}} is marked.

You can increase the number of {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}} slots you have available as you level up, to a maximum of 12.

A PC’s {{term:damage-thresholds|damage thresholds}} are calculated by adding their level to the listed {{term:damage-thresholds|damage thresholds}} of their equipped armor. A PC’s starting {{term:hit-points|HP}} is based on their class, but they can gain additional {{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} through advancements, features, and other effects.

An adversary’s {{term:damage-thresholds|Damage Thresholds}} and {{term:hit-points|HP}} are listed in their stat blocks.

When a character marks their last {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}}, they fall. If a PC falls, they make a {{term:death-move|death move}}.

Characters can clear {{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} by taking {{term:downtime|downtime moves}} (see: Downtime) or by activating relevant special abilities or effects.

**_Optional Rule: Massive Damage_**

If a character ever takes damage equal to twice their {{term:damage-thresholds|Severe threshold}}, they mark 4 {{term:hit-points|HP}} instead of 3.

name: Stress
text:
**{{term:stress|Stress}}** represents how much mental, physical, and emotional strain a character can endure. All classes start with 6 {{term:stress|Stress}} slots. You can increase the number of {{term:stress|Stress}} slots you have available as you level up, to a maximum of 12. Some special abilities or effects require the character activating them to mark {{term:stress|Stress}}, and the GM can require a PC to mark {{term:stress|Stress}} as a GM move or to represent the cost, complication, or consequence of an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}.

When a character marks their last {{term:stress|Stress}}, they become _{{term:vulnerable|Vulnerable}}_ (see: Conditions) until they clear at least 1 {{term:stress|Stress}}.

When a character must mark 1 or more {{term:stress|Stress}} but can’t, they mark 1 {{term:hit-points|HP}} instead. A character can’t use a move that requires them to mark {{term:stress|Stress}} if all of their {{term:stress|Stress}} is marked.

PCs can clear {{term:stress|Stress}} by making {{term:downtime|downtime moves}} (see: Downtime). A PC’s maximum {{term:stress|Stress}} is determined by their class, but they can increase it through advancements, abilities, and other effects.

name: Attacking
text:
### Attack Rolls

An **attack roll** is an {{term:action-roll|action roll}} intended to inflict harm. The trait that applies to an attack roll is specified by the weapon or spell being used. Unarmed attack rolls use either {{term:strength|Strength}} or {{term:finesse|Finesse}} (GM’s choice). An attack roll’s {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}}, unless otherwise noted, is equal to the {{term:difficulty|Difficulty}} score of its target.

### Damage Rolls

On a successful attack, roll damage. Damage is calculated from the **damage roll** listed in the attack’s description with the format “xdy+[modifier]” _(e.g., for a spell that inflicts “1d8+2”_ _damage, you roll an eight-sided and add 2 to the result; the_ _damage dealt is equal to the total)._

Any time an effect says to deal damage using your {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast trait}}, you roll a number of dice equal to your {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast trait}}.

**_Note:_** _If your {{term:spellcast-trait|Spellcast trait}} is +0 or lower, you don’t roll_ _anything._

For weapons, the number of damage dice you roll is equal to your **{{term:proficiency|Proficiency}}.** _Note that your {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} multiplies the_ _number of dice you roll, but doesn’t affect the modifier. For_ _example, a PC with {{term:proficiency|Proficiency}} 2 and wielding a weapon with a_ _damage rating of “d8+2” deals damage equal to “2d8+2” on a_ _successful attack._

Successful unarmed attacks inflict [{{term:proficiency|Proficiency}}]d4 damage.

### Critical Damage

When you get a {{term:critical-success|critical success}} (i.e., you roll matching values on your {{term:duality-dice|Duality Dice}}) on an attack roll, you deal extra damage. Make the damage roll as usual, but add the maximum possible result of the damage dice to the final total. For instance, if an attack would normally deal 2d8+1 damage, a {{term:critical-success|critical success}} would deal 2d8+1+16.

### Damage Types

There are two damage types: **physical damage (phy)** and **magic damage (mag)**. Unless stated otherwise, mundane weapons and unarmed attacks deal physical damage, and spells deal magic damage.

### Resistance, Immunity, and Direct Damage

If a target has **{{term:resistance|resistance}}** to a damage type, then they reduce {{term:incoming-damage|incoming damage}} of that type by half before comparing it to their {{term:hit-points|Hit Point}} Thresholds. If the target has additional ways of reducing {{term:incoming-damage|incoming damage}}, such as marking {{term:armor-slot|Armor Slots}}, they apply the {{term:resistance|resistance}} effect first. The effects of multiple resistances to the same damage type do not stack.

If a target has **{{term:immunity|immunity}}** to a damage type, they ignore {{term:incoming-damage|incoming damage}} of that type.

If an attack deals both physical and magic damage, a character can only benefit from {{term:resistance|resistance}} or {{term:immunity|immunity}} if they are resistant or {{term:immunity|immune}} to both damage types.

**{{term:direct-damage|Direct damage}}** is damage that can’t be reduced by marking {{term:armor-slot|Armor Slots}}.

### Multi-Target Attack Rolls

If a spell or ability allows you to target multiple adversaries, make one attack roll and one damage roll, then apply the results to each target individually.

### Multiple Damage Sources

Damage dealt simultaneously from multiple sources is always totaled before it’s compared to its target’s {{term:damage-thresholds|damage thresholds}}.

For example, if a PC with orc ancestry makes a successful attack against a target in {{term:melee|Melee range}} and decides to spend a {{term:hope|Hope}} to use their “Tusks” feature (which gives them an extra 1d6 damage on a damage roll), they would roll their normal weapon damage and add a d6 to the result, then deal that total damage to the adversary.

name: Maps, Range, and Movement
text:
You can play Daggerheart using “theater of the mind” or maps and miniatures. The conversions below from abstract ranges to physical measurements assume 1 inch of map represents about 5 feet of fictional space.

Daggerheart uses the following **ranges** to translate fictional positioning into relative distance for the purposes of targeting, movement, and other game mechanics:

**Melee:** Close enough to touch, up to a few feet away.

**Very Close:** Close enough to see fine details, about 5–10 feet away. While in danger, a character can move, as part of their action, from {{term:very-close|Very Close range}} into {{term:melee|Melee range}}. _On_ _a map: anything within the shortest length of a game card_ _(2-3 inches)._

**Close:** Close enough to see prominent details, about 10–30 feet away. While in danger, a character can move, as part of their action, from {{term:close|Close range}} into {{term:melee|Melee range}}. _On a_ _map: anything within the length of a pencil (5-6 inches)._

**Far:** Close enough to see very little detail, about 30–100 feet away. While in danger, a character must make an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll to safely move from {{term:far|Far range}} into {{term:melee|Melee range}}. _On a map: anything within the length of the long edge of a_ _piece of copy paper (11–12 inches)._

**Very Far:** Too far to make out any details, about 100–300 feet away. While in danger, a character must make an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll to safely move from {{term:very-far|Very Far range}} into {{term:melee|Melee range}}. _On a map: anything beyond {{term:far|Far range}}, but still within_ _the bounds of the conflict or scene._

**Out of Range:** Anything beyond a character’s {{term:very-far|Very Far range}} is Out of Range and usually can’t be targeted.

Range is measured from the source of an effect, such as the attacker or spellcaster, to the target or object of an effect.

A weapon, spell, ability, item, or other effect’s stated range is a maximum range; unless otherwise noted, it can be used at closer distances.

**Optional Rule: Defined Ranges**

_If your table would rather operate with more precise range_ _rules, you can use a 1-inch grid battle map during combat._ _If you do, use the following guidelines for play:_

- **Melee:** 1 square
- **Very Close:** 3 squares
- **Close:** 6 squares
- **Far:** 12 squares
- **Very Far:** 13+ squares
- **Out of Range:** Off the battlemap

### Movement Under Pressure

When you’re under pressure or in danger and make an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, you can move to a location within {{term:close|Close range}} as part of that action. If you’re not already making an {{term:action-roll|action roll}}, or if you want to move farther than your {{term:close|Close range}}, you need to succeed on an {{term:agility|Agility}} Roll to safely reposition yourself.

An adversary can move within {{term:close|Close range}} for free as part of an action, or within {{term:very-far|Very Far range}} as a separate action.

### Area of Effect

Unless stated otherwise, all the targets of a group effect must be within {{term:very-close|Very Close range}} of a single origin point within your effect’s range.

### Line of Sight & Cover

Unless stated otherwise, a ranged attacker must have **line** **of sight** to their intended target to make an attack roll. If a partial obstruction lies between the attacker and target, the target has **cover.** Attacks made through cover are rolled with {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}}. If the obstruction is total, there is no line of sight.

name: Conditions
text: **Conditions** are effects that grant specific benefits or drawbacks to the target they are attached to.

name: Standard Conditions
text:
Daggerheart has three standard conditions:

### Hidden

While you’re out of sight from all enemies and they don’t otherwise know your location, you gain the _{{term:hidden|Hidden}}_ condition. Any rolls against a _{{term:hidden|Hidden}}_ creature have {{term:disadvantage|disadvantage}}. After an adversary moves to where they would see you, you move into their line of sight, or you make an attack, you are no longer _{{term:hidden|Hidden}}_.

### Restrained

_{{term:restrained|Restrained}}_ characters can’t move, but you can still take actions from their current position.

### Vulnerable

When a creature is _{{term:vulnerable|Vulnerable}},_ all rolls targeting them have {{term:advantage|advantage}}.

Some features can apply special or unique conditions, which work as described in the feature text.

Unless otherwise noted, the same condition can’t be applied more than once to the same target.

name: Temporary Tags & Special Conditions
text:
The **{{term:temporary|temporary}}** tag denotes a condition or effect that the affected creature can clear by making a move against it. When an affected PC makes a move to clear a {{term:temporary|temporary}} condition or effect, it normally requires a successful {{term:action-roll|action roll}} using an appropriate trait. When an affected adversary makes a move to clear a {{term:temporary|temporary}} condition or effect, the GM puts the {{term:spotlight|spotlight}} on the adversary and describes how they do it; this doesn’t require a roll but it does use up that adversary’s {{term:spotlight|spotlight}}.

**Special conditions** are only cleared when specific requirements are met, such as completing a certain action or using a particular item. The requirements for clearing these conditions are stated in the text of the effect that applies the condition.

name: Downtime
text:
Between conflicts, the party can take a **rest** to recover expended resources and deepen their bonds. During a rest, each PC can make up to two {{term:downtime|downtime moves}}.

When the party rests, they must choose between a {{term:short-rest|short rest}} and a {{term:long-rest|long rest}}. If a party takes three {{term:short-rest|short rests}} in a row, their next rest must be a {{term:long-rest|long rest}}.

If a **{{term:short-rest|short rest}}** is interrupted, such as by an adversary's attack, the characters don’t gain its benefits. If a {{term:long-rest|long rest}} is interrupted, the characters only gain the benefits of a {{term:short-rest|short rest}}.

A **{{term:short-rest|short rest}}** lasts enough time for the party to catch its breath, about an hour in-world. Each player can move {{term:domain-card|domain cards}} between their {{term:loadout|loadout}} and {{term:vault|vault}} for free, then choose twice from the following list of {{term:downtime|downtime moves}} (players can choose the same move twice):

- **Tend to Wounds:** Clear 1d4+Tier {{term:hit-points|Hit Points}} for yourself or an ally.
- **Clear {{term:stress|Stress}}:** Clear 1d4+Tier {{term:stress|Stress}}.
- **Repair Armor:** Clear 1d4+Tier {{term:armor-slot|Armor Slots}} from your or an ally’s armor.
- **Prepare:** Describe how you prepare yourself for the path ahead, then gain a {{term:hope|Hope}}. If you choose to Prepare with one or more members of your party, you each gain 2 {{term:hope|Hope}}.
